title: Educational Amnesia: Why England Is Sleepwalking into a Scottish Mistake pwalking-into-a-scottish-mistake
author: Mark McCourt
summary: Mark McCourt argues that England is on the verge of repeating Scotland's Curriculum for Excellence (CfE) failure under a different name, even as English educators smugly point to CfE as a cautionary tale. He traces the mechanism: an anticipated change in education leadership favouring the same values-led, 'skills over knowledge' rhetoric that hollowed out CfE, compounded by Wales's Curriculum for Wales already replicating the same errors with one of CfE's own architects advising it. McCourt's deeper worry is not just political drift but institutional self-deception - schools and Multi-Academy Trusts that proclaim allegiance to 'knowledge-rich curriculum' often have shallow intellectual foundations and will wobble when the next appealingly-framed fad arrives. His proposed remedy is structural rather than personal: curricula and institutions built with genuine internal logic and intellectual depth that can resist ideological capture even as individual leaders and fashions change. The piece closes with McCourt's recurring theme that education's 30-year reform cycles are driven not by new ideas but by collective forgetting of what has already failed.
points: McCourt's central warning: England's curriculum and assessment review is on track to import a rebranded version of Scotland's failed Curriculum for Excellence, driven by the same 'skills over knowledge' ideology among incoming education leadership.

Wales has already fallen into the same trap - the Curriculum for Wales borrows heavily from CfE, including bringing on one of CfE's own architects as an advisor, replicating vague goals and weak knowledge progression.

McCourt's sharper critique: many self-described 'knowledge-rich' schools and Multi-Academy Trusts have only inherited the language of that principle, not its intellectual depth, making them vulnerable to the next fashionable reform.

His proposed solution is structural, not personal - curricula designed with internal logic, governance that prioritises intellectual depth, and training that builds genuine curricular expertise, because 'even the best people drift, or move on, or tire out.'

McCourt frames England's 30-year reform cycles as driven by institutional amnesia rather than genuine innovation: the system doesn't change because new ideas arrive, it changes because people forget what has already failed.
quotes: There's a strange psychological tick in education. We like to think of ourselves as rational, evidence-informed professionals who learn from failure. We even point, sometimes smugly, to the failures of others.
Ask any serious Scottish educator -- many MSPs included -- and you'll get the same verdict: CfE has been an unmitigated disaster. It failed to provide clarity, coherence, or direction.
Many individuals and institutions that loudly declare their allegiance to a "knowledge-rich curriculum" are far more vulnerable to educational fads than they realise.
This isn't hypocrisy so much as self-deception. People believe they are principled because they inherited the language of those principles.
We need structures that withstand the drift. Systems that outlast fashions. Institutions that resist ideological capture not by shouting louder, but by embodying a deeper coherence.
The education system doesn't change in 30-year cycles because new ideas come along. It changes in cycles because people forget.
